topics.title: The particle model
topics.intro: Everything is made of tiny particles. The way they are arranged and move explains solids, liquids, gases, smells spreading and balloons bursting.
topics.teach: Explain why you can smell perfume from across a room.
topics.talk: Ask her why a balloon gets bigger in the sun.

topics.title: Cells and the microscope
topics.intro: All living things are made of cells, the building blocks of life. Most are far too small to see without a microscope.
topics.teach: Explain three differences between a plant cell and an animal cell.
topics.hook: Cells are the building blocks of life, and **mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell**.

topics.title: Atoms, elements and compounds
topics.intro: There are only about 118 elements, but they combine to make everything in the universe.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between an element and a compound.
topics.hook: Element: one kind of atom. Compound: different atoms **chemically joined**. Mixture: just **mixed**.

topics.title: Mixtures and separating them
topics.intro: Sea water, ink and air are all mixtures. Scientists have clever ways to separate them.
topics.teach: Explain how you could get pure water from sea water.
topics.talk: Ask her what “pure” means to a scientist.
topics.hook: **Filter** out bits, **evaporate** to get a solid back, **distil** to get a liquid back, **chromatography** for colours.

topics.title: Acids and alkalis
topics.intro: Lemon juice, soap, vinegar and toothpaste: some are acids and some are alkalis. Indicators tell them apart.
topics.teach: Explain what happens when an acid and an alkali are mixed.
topics.talk: Ask her why indigestion tablets help with heartburn.
topics.hook: pH **7** is neutral: below 7 is acid (sour), above 7 is alkali (soapy).

topics.title: Forces and motion
topics.intro: Forces change how things move. Now we’ll calculate speed and weight, and read distance–time graphs.
topics.teach: Explain what balanced forces do to a moving object.
topics.talk: Ask her what your speed is if you drive 120 km in 2 hours.
topics.hook: **Balanced** forces: no change in motion. **Unbalanced**: speed up, slow down or change direction.

topics.title: Energy stores and resources
topics.intro: Energy is never used up. It moves between stores: kinetic, thermal, chemical and more.
topics.teach: Explain the energy changes when you throw a ball up in the air.
topics.talk: Ask her which energy resources are renewable.
topics.hook: Energy is never used up, only **moved between stores**, like money moved between bank accounts.

topics.title: Stars, galaxies and the solar system
topics.intro: Our Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars in the Milky Way, and the Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies.
topics.talk: Ask her what causes a solar eclipse.
topics.hook: Planet → solar system → galaxy → universe: like house → street → town → world.

topics.title: Food webs and photosynthesis
topics.intro: Every living thing depends on others. Energy flows from the Sun through plants to animals.
topics.teach: Explain what would happen to a food web if all the bees disappeared.
topics.talk: Ask her where a tree gets the stuff to build its trunk.
topics.hook: Sun → plant → animal: the arrows point to the **eater**, following the energy.

topics.title: Reproduction in plants and animals
topics.intro: All living things reproduce. Flowers are a plant’s way of making seeds.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between pollination and fertilisation.
topics.talk: Ask her how a sycamore seed travels.
topics.hook: First **pollination** (pollen lands), then **fertilisation** (cells join), then **dispersal** (seeds travel).

topics.title: Investigations: fair tests and results
topics.intro: Scientists test ideas with fair tests: change one thing, measure another, and keep everything else the same.
topics.teach: Explain how to make an investigation a fair test.
topics.talk: Plan a kitchen experiment together: which variable will you change?
topics.hook: **Cows Moo Softly**: **C**hange one thing, **M**easure one thing, keep everything else the **S**ame.

items.prompt: When a metal bar is heated it expands (gets slightly longer). Why?

options.text: The particles vibrate more and spread apart
Each particle swells and gets a little bigger
options.feedback: A very common idea! The particles themselves stay the same size. They take up more room because they move more.

options.text: The heat makes extra particles in the metal
options.feedback: Heating doesn’t create particles; the number stays the same.

items.explain: Heating gives particles more energy, so they vibrate more and need more space. The particles do not grow.
items.hook: Particles never grow: heated, they **jiggle** more and need more room.
items.example: Bridges and railway tracks have small gaps so they can expand on hot days without buckling.

items.prompt: What is in the space between the particles of a gas?

options.text: Nothing at all
Air, which fills the gaps
options.feedback: Air IS a gas, made of particles. Between the particles there is nothing at all.

options.text: Water vapour
options.feedback: Water vapour is itself made of particles.

items.explain: Gas particles are far apart with empty space (a vacuum) between them, which is why gases can be squashed.
items.hook: Between gas particles there is **nothing**: just empty space.
items.example: Block the end of a bike pump and push: the air squashes because there is empty space between its particles.

items.explain: In a solid, particles are packed in a regular pattern and vibrate on the spot.
items.choosePrompt: Which state of matter is highlighted?
items.locatePrompt: Tap the box showing a solid.
items.hook: Solid: particles in neat rows, **vibrating on the spot**, like fidgety pupils sitting in assembly.
items.example: An ice cube keeps its shape until it starts to melt.

items.explain: In a liquid, particles touch but are jumbled and can slide past each other, so liquids flow.
items.choosePrompt: Which state of matter is highlighted?
items.locatePrompt: Tap the box showing a liquid.
items.hook: Liquid: particles **touching but sliding** past each other, like people in a busy corridor.
items.example: Pour juice from a carton into a glass: it flows and takes the shape of the glass.

items.explain: In a gas, particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions.
items.choosePrompt: Which state of matter is highlighted?
items.locatePrompt: Tap the box showing a gas.
items.hook: Gas: particles **far apart and zooming** in all directions, like a playground at break time.
items.example: Air from a pump spreads into every part of a bike tyre.

items.prompt: What is the spreading out of particles from where there are lots to where there are fewer called?
items.explain: Diffusion is why you can smell food cooking from another room. It happens faster in warm gases.
items.hook: Diffusion: particles spread from crowded to empty, like people leaving a packed lift.
items.example: You can smell toast from upstairs, and a drop of squash slowly colours a whole glass of water.

items.prompt: Why can a gas be squashed (compressed) but a liquid hardly at all?
distractors: gas particles are soft and squashy
items.explain: In a liquid the particles already touch, so there is no room to squash them closer.
items.hook: A gas has room to squash; a liquid is already packed tight.
items.example: A bike pump squashes air into a tyre, but you can’t squash water in a sealed syringe.

items.prompt: What causes the pressure of a gas inside a balloon?
items.answer: gas particles hitting the inside walls
items.explain: Billions of collisions every second push the balloon outwards. Heating makes them move faster and hit harder.
items.hook: Gas pressure = billions of tiny particle punches on the walls every second.
items.example: A football left in hot sun feels harder: the warmer air particles hit the inside faster and harder.

items.prompt: When a solid turns straight into a gas without melting, it is called…
items.explain: Dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) sublimes, making the “smoke” used on stage.
items.hook: Sublimation **skips the liquid**: solid straight to gas.
items.example: On cold, dry, sunny days, snow can slowly vanish without melting first: it sublimes.

items.prompt: Which state of matter has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container?
items.explain: Liquids keep their volume but flow to fill the bottom of a container. Gases fill the whole container.
items.hook: Liquids keep their **volume** but borrow their container’s **shape**.
items.example: 500 ml of water is still 500 ml in a tall glass or a wide bowl.

items.prompt: Why does ice float on water?
items.answer: ice is less dense than liquid water
distractors: ice is lighter because it is cold
items.explain: Water is unusual: as it freezes, its particles form an open pattern that takes up more space, so ice is less dense.
items.hook: Water is the odd one out: its solid floats on its liquid.
items.example: Ice cubes float in a drink, and ponds freeze from the top down, so fish survive underneath.

items.prompt: Do plant cells have mitochondria?

options.text: Yes: plants respire to release energy, just like animals
No: plants get energy by photosynthesis instead
options.feedback: Plants photosynthesise to make food (glucose), but they still need mitochondria to release the energy from it by respiration, day and night.

options.text: Only plants that live in the dark
options.feedback: All plant cells that are alive respire.

items.explain: Photosynthesis makes glucose; respiration in the mitochondria releases its energy. Plants do both.
items.hook: Photosynthesis **makes** the food; respiration **releases** its energy. Plants do both.

items.prompt: Which of these is made of cells?

options.text: All living things, including you
Only animals, not plants or fungi
options.feedback: Plants, fungi and bacteria are all made of cells too.

options.text: Only things you can see moving
options.feedback: Trees don’t move about but are made of billions of cells.

items.explain: Every living thing is made of one or more cells. That is one of the big ideas of biology.
items.hook: **All** living things are made of cells: a bacterium is one cell; you are about 37 trillion.
items.example: Even the mould on old bread and the moss on a wall are made of cells.

items.explain: The nucleus controls the cell and contains genetic material (DNA).
items.hook: The nucleus is the cell’s **control centre**, holding the instructions (DNA).

items.explain: Cytoplasm is the jelly where most of the cell’s chemical reactions happen.
items.hook: Cytoplasm is the cell’s jelly-like kitchen, where most reactions are cooked up.

items.explain: The cell membrane controls what goes in and out of the cell.
items.hook: The membrane is the cell’s **security guard**, deciding what goes in and out.

items.explain: Mitochondria are where respiration happens, releasing energy.
items.hook: **Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell.**
items.example: Muscle cells, which work hard, are packed with extra mitochondria.

items.explain: The cell wall is made of cellulose. It is strong and supports the plant cell. Animal cells don’t have one.
items.hook: A cell **wall** is a strong box around a plant cell, made of cellulose.
items.example: Paper and cotton are made of cellulose, the same stuff as plant cell walls.

items.explain: Chloroplasts contain green chlorophyll and are where photosynthesis happens.
items.hook: **Chloro-** means green: green chloroplasts catch sunlight for photosynthesis.
items.example: Leaves are green because their cells are packed with chloroplasts; roots underground have none.

items.explain: The vacuole is filled with cell sap and keeps the cell firm.
items.hook: The vacuole is the cell’s **water balloon**: full of sap, keeping it firm.
items.example: A droopy pot plant perks up after watering as its vacuoles fill up again.

items.prompt: What do ribosomes do?
items.explain: Ribosomes are tiny structures that build proteins.
items.hook: Ribosomes are tiny **protein factories**.

items.prompt: Which three parts do plant cells have that animal cells do not?
items.answer: cell wall, chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole
items.explain: Both have a nucleus, cytoplasm, membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes.
items.hook: Plant extras: a **wall** to stand tall, **chloroplasts** to catch light, a **vacuole** to stay firm.

items.prompt: Who first used the word “cell” after looking at cork through a microscope in 1665?
items.explain: Hooke thought the tiny boxes in cork looked like the small rooms (cells) monks lived in.
items.hook: **Hooke** looked at cork and saw rows of tiny rooms, like monks’ **cells**.
items.example: A cork from a bottle is the same material Hooke looked at.

items.prompt: A microscope has a ×10 eyepiece and a ×40 objective lens. What is the total magnification?
items.explain: Total magnification = eyepiece × objective = 10 × 40 = 400.
items.hook: Total magnification: **multiply**, don’t add. Eyepiece × objective.
items.example: Under ×400, a hair about a tenth of a millimetre wide would look 4 centimetres wide.

items.prompt: Put these in order, from smallest to largest.
items.explain: Cells group into tissues, tissues into organs, organs into organ systems, and systems make an organism.
items.hook: Bricks → walls → rooms → floors → house: cell → tissue → organ → system → organism.

items.prompt: Which specialised cell has no nucleus, leaving more room to carry oxygen?
items.explain: Red blood cells are packed with haemoglobin, which carries oxygen.
items.hook: Red blood cells ditch the nucleus to make room for more oxygen-carrying haemoglobin.
items.example: Blood is red because of the iron-containing haemoglobin in red blood cells.

items.prompt: Which plant cell has a long thin extension to absorb water from the soil?
items.explain: The long “hair” gives a large surface area for absorbing water and minerals.
items.hook: Root hair cells are long thin straws in the soil, drinking up water.
items.example: Gently pull up a seedling grown on damp kitchen roll: the fuzz on its roots is root hairs.

items.prompt: Which cell is long and thin to carry electrical signals around the body?
items.explain: Some nerve cells are over a metre long, running from your spine to your toes.
items.hook: Nerve cells are the body’s **wires**: long and thin to carry electrical signals.
items.example: Stub your toe and a signal races along nerve cells up your leg to your spinal cord.

items.prompt: Is a compound the same as a mixture?

options.text: No: a compound’s elements are chemically joined
Yes, they are two words for the same thing
options.feedback: They are very different. Iron and sulfur mixed can be separated with a magnet; iron sulfide, a compound, cannot.

options.text: Only when both are liquids at room temperature
options.feedback: The difference is about chemical bonds, not the state.

items.explain: Water (H₂O) is a compound: hydrogen and oxygen are chemically bonded. Air is a mixture of different gases.
items.hook: Mixture = just **mixed**, easy to separate. Compound = **chemically joined**: a new substance.
items.example: Iron filings and sulfur separate with a magnet; heat them and they make iron sulfide, which won’t.

items.prompt: A substance made of only one type of atom is called…
items.explain: Gold, oxygen and carbon are elements.
items.hook: Element = **one** kind of atom only, like a box of identical Lego bricks.
items.example: The copper in electric wires, the carbon in pencil “lead” (graphite) and the helium in a balloon are elements.

items.prompt: A substance made of two or more elements chemically joined is called…
items.explain: Water, carbon dioxide and salt are compounds.
items.hook: **Com**pound = **com**bined: different atoms bonded into a new substance.
items.example: Table salt is sodium (a metal that fizzes on water) joined to chlorine (a poisonous gas), yet you sprinkle it on chips.

items.prompt: Roughly how many elements are known?
items.explain: About 118, of which around 90 occur naturally.
items.example: Everything you can see, from your desk to your dinner to you, is built from combinations of these elements.

items.prompt: Which scientist arranged the elements into the first periodic table in 1869, leaving gaps for undiscovered ones?
items.explain: Mendeleev’s gaps were later filled by elements with the properties he predicted.
items.hook: Mendeleev is said to have sorted cards of the elements like a game of patience, leaving gaps for missing ones.

items.prompt: What is the chemical symbol for oxygen?
items.explain: Oxygen is O. H is hydrogen, C is carbon, N is nitrogen.
items.hook: Many symbols start with the element’s first letter: **O**xygen, **H**ydrogen, **C**arbon, **N**itrogen.
items.example: Oxygen cylinders in hospitals and ambulances are labelled O₂.

items.prompt: Which element has the symbol Na?
items.explain: Na comes from its Latin name, natrium.
items.hook: **Na** from **na**trium. Sodium is the Na in NaCl, table salt.
items.example: Old orange street lights in the UK were sodium lamps.

items.prompt: Which element has the symbol Fe?
items.explain: Fe comes from the Latin ferrum. “Ferrous” metals contain iron.
items.hook: **Fe** from **fe**rrum. “Ferrous” metals contain iron.
items.example: Breakfast cereal boxes often say “fortified with iron”: check the label.

items.prompt: Which element has the symbol Au?
items.explain: Au from aurum, Latin for gold. Silver is Ag (argentum).
items.hook: **Au**: “**A**y, yo**u**! Give me back my gold!”
items.example: Olympic gold medals are mostly silver with a coating of gold.

items.prompt: What does the formula H₂O tell you about a water molecule?
items.answer: it has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom
distractors: it has 2 oxygen atoms and 1 hydrogen atom
it has 2 hydrogen molecules and an oxygen gas
items.explain: The small 2 belongs to the H in front of it.
items.hook: The little number belongs to the atom **just before** it: H₂O = two H, one O.
items.example: People often call water “H-two-O” in everyday speech.

items.prompt: What is the formula of carbon dioxide?
items.explain: One carbon atom and two oxygen atoms (di- means two).
items.hook: **Di-** means two: carbon **di**oxide has two oxygens, just as a **di**lemma has two options.
items.example: The bubbles in fizzy drinks are carbon dioxide.

items.prompt: Which gas makes up about 78% of the air?
items.explain: Air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 1% other gases including carbon dioxide.
items.hook: Air is nearly **four-fifths nitrogen** and about one-fifth oxygen.
items.example: Crisp packets are often filled with nitrogen to keep the crisps fresh.

items.prompt: On the periodic table, where are most metals found?
distractors: only along the bottom two rows
items.explain: Non-metals are on the right. The staircase line separates them.
items.hook: Metals on the **left** and middle; non-metals on the **right**; the staircase is the border.

items.prompt: A carton says “100% pure orange juice”. To a scientist, is it a pure substance?

options.text: No: it is a mixture of substances
Yes, because nothing has been added to it
options.feedback: In everyday language “pure” means nothing added. In science a pure substance contains only one substance.

options.text: Yes, as long as it is freshly squeezed
options.feedback: Fresh juice is still a mixture of many substances.

items.explain: A pure substance contains only one element or compound, and melts and boils at fixed temperatures.
items.hook: Science “pure” = **one substance only**. Shop “pure” = nothing added.
items.example: Even bottled spring water contains dissolved minerals: check the label.

items.prompt: In salt water, the salt is the solute. What is the water?
items.explain: Solute + solvent = solution.
items.hook: Solute + solvent = solution. The solvent is the liquid that does the dissolving.
items.example: In a glass of squash, water is the solvent and the sugar is a solute.

items.prompt: A solution in which no more solute can dissolve is called…
items.explain: Warming the solvent usually lets more solid dissolve.
items.hook: Saturated = **full up**, like a soaked sponge that can’t hold any more.
items.example: Keep stirring sugar into cold water and eventually grains stay at the bottom: it’s saturated.

items.prompt: Which method could get pure drinking water from sea water?
items.explain: Distillation boils the water off and condenses the steam, leaving the salt behind.
items.hook: Distillation: **boil it, cool it, collect it**.
items.example: Sea water evaporates in the sunshine and falls as fresh rain: the water cycle is nature’s distillation.

items.prompt: Which method separates the different coloured dyes in an ink?
items.explain: The dyes travel up the paper at different speeds, so they separate.
items.hook: **Chroma** means colour: chromatography is “colour writing”.
items.example: Draw a black felt-tip dot on kitchen roll, dip the edge in water and watch hidden colours spread out.

items.prompt: How can you get large crystals of salt from salt solution?
items.explain: Slow evaporation gives the crystals time to grow.
items.hook: Slow and steady grows big crystals; rush it and you get tiny ones.
items.example: Sugar crystals grown on a string over several days get big and chunky.

items.prompt: How can a scientist test whether a substance is pure?
items.answer: check it melts at one exact temperature
distractors: check that it tastes the same throughout
see whether it is clear and see-through
weigh it before and after heating
items.explain: Pure water boils at exactly 100°C; impurities change and spread out the boiling and melting points.
items.hook: Pure = sharp: it melts or boils at **one exact temperature**.
items.example: Gritting roads with salt makes ice melt below 0°C: an impurity changes the melting point.

items.prompt: To get pure salt from rock salt (salt mixed with sand), put the steps in order.
items.explain: The salt dissolves but the sand does not. Filter, then evaporate the filtrate to get the salt back.
items.hook: Crush, Dissolve, Filter, Evaporate: “**C**ats **D**on’t **F**ancy **E**lephants”.
items.example: The rock salt spread on icy UK roads in winter is mined in Cheshire: salt mixed with sand and clay.

items.prompt: Are all acids dangerous?

options.text: No: some, like vinegar, are safe to eat
Yes, all acids burn your skin badly
options.feedback: Strong acids are dangerous, but weak acids are in lots of foods.

options.text: Only the acids that are brightly coloured
options.feedback: Colour has nothing to do with it.

items.explain: Strong acids (like concentrated hydrochloric acid) are corrosive. Weak acids give food a sour taste.
items.hook: Sour = acid. Many weak acids are safe to eat.
items.example: Vinegar on your chips is a weak acid (ethanoic acid); lemon juice contains citric acid.

items.hook: pH **7** is neutral: **below** 7 is acid, **above** 7 is alkali.
items.example: Lemon juice is about pH 2, pure water pH 7 and soap about pH 9 to 10.

items.prompt: The pH scale runs from 0 to…
items.explain: pH 0 to 14: below 7 acid, 7 neutral, above 7 alkali.
items.hook: 0 to 14, with **7** right in the middle for neutral.
items.example: Lemon juice is about pH 2, pure water pH 7 and soap about pH 9 to 10.

items.prompt: What colour does an acid turn blue litmus paper?
items.explain: Acids turn blue litmus red; alkalis turn red litmus blue.
items.hook: **BRA**: **B**lue litmus turns **R**ed in **A**cid.
items.example: Red cabbage water is a homemade indicator: lemon juice turns it pink; bicarbonate of soda turns it blue-green.

items.prompt: Acid + alkali → ? + water
items.explain: Neutralisation makes a salt and water. Hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride (table salt) + water.
items.hook: Acid + alkali → salt + water: they cancel each other out.
items.example: Farmers spread lime (an alkali) on fields to neutralise acidic soil.

items.prompt: Which acid does your stomach make to help digest food and kill bacteria?
items.explain: Stomach acid has a pH of about 1 to 2.
items.example: The burning feeling of heartburn is stomach acid creeping up into the food pipe.

items.prompt: Why do indigestion tablets work?
distractors: they add more acid to digest the food
they cool and calm the stomach lining
they coat the stomach with sugar
items.explain: Neutralisation in everyday life!
items.hook: Too much acid? Add a base to neutralise it.
items.example: Many indigestion tablets contain calcium carbonate, the same chemical as chalk.

items.prompt: A hazard symbol showing liquid eating through a hand and a surface means…
items.explain: Corrosive substances destroy living tissue and materials. Wear goggles!
items.hook: **Corrosive** things **corrode**: they eat away skin and metal.
items.example: Some oven cleaners and drain unblockers carry the corrosive symbol.

items.prompt: A car moves along a straight road at a steady 30 mph. What can you say about the forces on it?

options.text: They are balanced: the driving force equals the resistive forces
The forward force must be bigger, or it would stop
options.feedback: If the forward force were bigger the car would speed up. Steady speed means balanced forces.

options.text: There are no forces on it
options.feedback: There are forces (engine, friction, air resistance); they just cancel out.

items.explain: Balanced forces mean no change in motion: stay still, or keep moving at the same speed in the same direction.
items.hook: Steady speed in a straight line = **balanced** forces. No overall force, no change.
items.example: At a steady 70 mph on a motorway, the engine’s push exactly matches air resistance and friction.

items.hook: **Speed = distance ÷ time.** In the triangle, D sits on top of S and T.
items.example: UK speed limits are in mph: miles per hour, a distance divided by a time.

items.hook: **Weight = mass × g**, and on Earth g is about 10 N/kg.
items.example: A 1 kg bag of sugar weighs about 10 N on Earth, but only 1.6 N on the Moon.

items.prompt: A box has 10 N pushing it right and 4 N friction pulling left. What is the resultant force?
items.explain: Opposite forces subtract: 10 − 4 = 6 N, in the direction of the bigger force.
items.hook: Same direction: **add**. Opposite directions: **subtract**, and it goes the way of the bigger force.
items.example: In tug of war, the team pulling harder wins: the resultant force points their way.

items.prompt: On a distance–time graph, what does a flat (horizontal) line mean?
distractors: it is moving at a steady high speed
it is going back towards the start
items.explain: Distance isn’t changing, so it has stopped. A steeper line means faster.
items.hook: Flat line: time ticks on but distance doesn’t, so it has **stopped**.
items.example: A bus waiting at a stop makes a flat line on its distance–time graph.

items.prompt: On a distance–time graph, a steeper straight line means…
items.explain: More distance in the same time = faster.
items.hook: **Steeper = speedier.**
items.example: A cyclist racing downhill makes a steeper line than someone pushing a bike uphill.

items.prompt: If you double the force on a spring (without overstretching it), its extension…
items.explain: Hooke’s law: extension is proportional to force, up to the limit of proportionality.
items.hook: Hooke’s law: **double the pull, double the stretch**. (The same Robert Hooke named cells!)
items.example: Overstretch a hair bobble or a spring and it won’t go back to its old shape: it has passed its limit.

items.prompt: An astronaut goes from Earth to the Moon. What happens to her mass?
items.explain: Mass is the amount of matter and doesn’t change. Her weight is about one-sixth.
items.hook: Mass stays, weight changes: same **stuff**, different **pull**.

items.prompt: When a phone battery goes flat, what has happened to the energy?

options.text: It has been transferred to other stores, mostly heating the surroundings
It has been used up and no longer exists
options.feedback: Energy is never destroyed. It is transferred, and much of it ends up as thermal energy in the surroundings (dissipated).

options.text: It has turned into electricity and gone back into the plug
options.feedback: It doesn’t go back to the plug.

items.explain: The law of conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores.
items.hook: Energy is never destroyed: much of it ends up **spread out as heat** (dissipated).
items.example: A phone or laptop feels warm when it’s working hard: energy is heating the surroundings.

items.prompt: What unit is energy measured in?
items.explain: Energy in joules (J). Power, the rate of energy transfer, is in watts (W).
items.hook: Joules = **how much** energy. Watts = **how fast** (joules per second).
items.example: UK food labels show energy in kJ (kilojoules) as well as kcal.

items.prompt: A moving object has energy in which store?
items.explain: The faster it moves, the more energy in its kinetic store.
items.hook: **Kinetic** and **cinema** both come from the Greek for movement.
items.example: A football flying towards the goal has energy in its kinetic store.

items.prompt: A book lifted onto a high shelf gains energy in which store?
items.explain: The higher it is raised, the more energy in its gravitational potential store.
items.hook: Higher up = more gravitational potential energy, waiting to fall.
items.example: A rollercoaster’s first big climb fills its gravitational store for the rest of the ride.

items.prompt: Food, fuels and batteries all store energy in which store?
items.explain: Chemical reactions transfer this energy, for example respiration in your cells.
items.hook: Chemical store: energy locked in food, fuels and batteries, released by reactions.
items.example: A burning log, a car’s petrol and the cereal you eat for breakfast all transfer energy from chemical stores.

items.prompt: A stretched catapult elastic stores energy in which store?
items.explain: When released, the energy is transferred to the kinetic store of the stone.
items.hook: Stretch it or squash it, and it stores elastic potential energy to spring back.
items.example: A trampoline stores energy as it stretches down, then bounces you back up.

items.prompt: Which of these energy resources is renewable?
items.explain: Renewables (wind, solar, hydroelectric, tidal, geothermal, biomass) won’t run out.
items.hook: **Re-new-able**: nature tops it up. Fossil fuels took millions of years to form.
items.example: Huge offshore wind farms in the North Sea now generate a large share of the UK’s electricity.

items.prompt: Burning fossil fuels releases which gas that contributes to climate change?
items.explain: Coal, oil and gas formed from ancient living things. Burning them releases carbon dioxide.
items.hook: Fossil fuels are ancient life, buried and squashed. Burn them and their carbon returns as CO₂.
items.example: A gas hob burns natural gas (methane), releasing carbon dioxide and water.

items.prompt: What unit is power measured in?
items.explain: A 60 W bulb transfers 60 joules every second.
items.hook: **1 watt = 1 joule every second.**
items.example: A UK kettle is about 3000 W; an LED light bulb is about 5 to 10 W.

items.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up and caught. Put the main energy stores in order.
items.explain: Chemical → kinetic → gravitational potential → kinetic. Some energy is dissipated to the surroundings by air resistance.
items.hook: Muscles → rising → top → falling: **chemical, kinetic, gravitational, kinetic**.
items.example: Throw a ball up in the garden: it slows, pauses for a split second at the top, then speeds up as it falls.

items.prompt: Is the Sun the biggest star in the universe?

options.text: No: it is an average-sized star
Yes, that is why it looks so bright
options.feedback: It looks bright because it is close. Some stars are over 1000 times wider than the Sun.

options.text: The Sun is a planet, not a star
options.feedback: The Sun is a star, the closest one to us.

items.explain: The Sun looks biggest and brightest only because it is about 150 million km away; the next nearest star is about 40 trillion km away.
items.hook: The Sun is an ordinary star that just lives next door.
items.example: A torch held near you looks brighter than a distant lighthouse: being close makes the Sun look special.

items.prompt: A light-year is a measure of…

options.text: distance
time
options.feedback: Despite the name, it is a distance, about 9.5 trillion km.

options.text: brightness
options.feedback: It measures distance, not brightness.

items.explain: Light travels about 300 000 km every second, so in a year it goes about 9.5 trillion km.
items.hook: A light-**year** sounds like time, but it’s a **distance**: how far light goes in a year.
items.example: Looking at the stars is looking back in time: you see light that left them years ago.

items.prompt: What is the name of our galaxy?
items.explain: The Milky Way contains hundreds of billions of stars. Andromeda is our nearest large neighbouring galaxy.
items.hook: **Galaxy** comes from the Greek for milk, so “Milky Way galaxy” says milk twice!
items.example: From a dark place such as Northumberland or Exmoor you can see the Milky Way as a misty band across the sky.

items.prompt: After the Sun, which is the nearest star to Earth?
items.explain: Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light-years away.
items.hook: **Proxima** is Latin for “nearest”, as in **proximity**.

items.prompt: About how long does light from the Sun take to reach Earth?
items.explain: So when you see the Sun, you see it as it was about 8 minutes ago. (Never look straight at it!)
items.hook: Sunlight takes about **8 minutes** to reach us: about as long as hard-boiling an egg.

items.prompt: What keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
items.explain: The Sun’s gravity pulls on the planets, bending their paths into orbits.
items.hook: Gravity is like an invisible string: swing a ball on a string, let go, and it flies off.

items.prompt: A solar eclipse happens when…
items.answer: the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth
distractors: the Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon
the Sun passes behind a planet
items.explain: In a lunar eclipse, the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon.
items.hook: **Solar**: Moon in the middle, blocking the Sun. **Lunar**: Earth in the middle, shadowing the Moon.
items.example: The UK saw a deep partial solar eclipse on 20 March 2015; the next total one visible here is in 2090.

items.prompt: The asteroid belt lies between which two planets?
items.explain: Millions of rocky asteroids orbit there.
items.hook: The asteroid belt is a rocky fence between the four rocky planets and the four giants.

items.prompt: Which two planets are “gas giants”?
items.explain: Jupiter and Saturn are mostly hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune are “ice giants”.
items.hook: Jupiter and Saturn: **gas giants**. Uranus and Neptune: **ice giants**.
items.example: Through a small telescope or good binoculars you can spot Saturn’s rings and Jupiter’s moons.

items.prompt: Where does a tree get most of the material to build its trunk and leaves?

options.text: From carbon dioxide in the air
From minerals in the soil
options.feedback: A common idea! In the 1600s van Helmont grew a willow tree for 5 years: it gained about 74 kg, but the soil lost only about 60 g.

options.text: From water taken up by its roots
options.feedback: Water matters, but most of the dry mass comes from carbon in carbon dioxide.

items.explain: Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, using light energy. The plant builds itself from that glucose.
items.hook: A tree is built mostly from **thin air**: carbon dioxide (plus water).
items.example: Burning a log puts the carbon the tree took from the air back into the air as carbon dioxide.

items.prompt: In the food chain grass → rabbit → fox, what do the arrows show?

options.text: The direction energy flows
Which animal eats which, pointing at the food
options.feedback: The arrow points TO the eater, showing where the energy goes.

options.text: Which living thing is biggest
options.feedback: Arrows are about energy transfer, not size.

items.explain: Arrows always point from the thing eaten to the eater.
items.hook: Arrows point to the **eater**: read them as “gives energy to”.

items.prompt: In a food chain, what is a green plant called?
items.explain: Producers make their own food by photosynthesis. Every food chain starts with one.
items.hook: **Producers produce** their own food using sunlight.
items.example: Grass in a field, vegetables in a garden and seaweed on a beach are all producers.

items.prompt: Complete the word equation: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + ?
items.explain: Photosynthesis releases the oxygen we breathe.
items.hook: **Photo** = light, **synthesis** = making: making food with light.
items.example: Pondweed in sunlight gives off tiny bubbles: that is oxygen from photosynthesis.

items.prompt: Which green chemical in leaves absorbs light for photosynthesis?
items.explain: Chlorophyll is found inside chloroplasts.
items.hook: Chloro**phyll** is the green **pigment**; chloro**plasts** are the little packets that hold it.
items.example: Leaves turn yellow and red in autumn as the green chlorophyll breaks down.

items.prompt: An animal that eats only plants is called a…
items.explain: Rabbits, deer and cows are herbivores.
items.hook: **Herb**ivores eat plants, **carn**ivores eat meat (as in chilli con **carn**e), **omni**vores eat all.
items.example: Sheep and cows grazing on British hillsides are herbivores.

items.prompt: Fungi and bacteria that break down dead material are called…
items.explain: Decomposers return nutrients to the soil for plants to use again.
items.hook: Decomposers are nature’s recyclers, rotting dead things back into nutrients.
items.example: A compost heap, mushrooms on a rotting log and mould on old bread are decomposers at work.

items.prompt: In a woodland food web, a disease kills most of the owls, which eat mice. What happens to the mice first?

options.text: Their numbers increase
They all die from the same disease
options.feedback: The mice don’t catch the owls’ disease; they lose a predator.

options.text: Their numbers stay exactly the same
options.feedback: Living things in a food web depend on each other (interdependence).

items.explain: Then, with more mice, the plants and seeds they eat may decrease. Changes ripple through the web.
items.hook: Lose a predator and the prey boom; everything in a food web is linked.

items.prompt: Why are bees so important to many food crops?
distractors: they eat the pests that harm crops
they carry water to the plants
items.explain: About a third of the food we eat depends on pollinators.
items.hook: Bees are flying pollen couriers, carrying pollen from flower to flower.
items.example: Apples, strawberries and blackberries all crop better when bees visit their flowers.

items.prompt: Put this food chain in order, starting with the producer.
items.explain: Energy flows from the producer through each consumer in turn.
items.hook: Every food chain starts with a **producer**, then the arrows point to whoever eats it.
items.example: In a seaside rock pool: seaweed → periwinkles → shore crabs → gulls.

items.prompt: Why do many flowers have brightly coloured petals and a sweet scent?

options.text: To attract insects that carry pollen
To scare away animals that eat them
options.feedback: The colours and scents attract animals; they don’t scare them.

options.text: Just to look pretty for people
options.feedback: Flowers evolved long before people. The colours attract pollinators.

items.explain: Insect-pollinated flowers offer nectar as a reward. Wind-pollinated flowers, like grasses, are small and dull.
items.hook: Bright colours and sweet scents are adverts saying: “Free nectar here!”
items.example: Bees buzzing round lavender in a summer garden are drinking nectar and carrying pollen.

items.explain: Petals are often brightly coloured to attract insects.
items.hook: Petals are the flower’s **billboard**, advertising nectar to insects.

items.explain: Sepals protect the flower when it is a bud.
items.hook: Sepals are the bud’s **protective jacket**: the green leafy bits under the petals.
items.example: The green leafy frill on top of a strawberry is its sepals.

items.explain: The anther makes pollen, which carries the male sex cells. Anther + filament = stamen.
items.hook: The stamen (anther + filament) is the male part: think “sta-**MEN**”.
items.example: Lily anthers drop orange pollen that stains clothes, so florists often snip them off.

items.explain: The filament is the stalk that holds up the anther.
items.hook: Filament = a thin stalk, like the thin glowing filament wire in an old light bulb.

items.explain: The sticky stigma catches pollen.
items.hook: The **st**igma is **st**icky, to catch pollen.

items.explain: The style connects the stigma to the ovary.
items.hook: The style is the neck between stigma and ovary: pollen tubes grow down it.

items.explain: The ovary contains ovules, which hold the female sex cells. Stigma + style + ovary = carpel.
items.hook: After fertilisation the ovary becomes the **fruit** and the ovules become **seeds**.
items.example: A pea pod is a ripened ovary, and the peas inside were its ovules.

items.prompt: The transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma is called…
items.explain: Pollination comes first; fertilisation happens later, when the pollen nucleus joins the ovule nucleus.
items.hook: **P**ollen lands first (**p**ollination); **f**usion of the cells comes later (**f**ertilisation).
items.example: Hay fever is caused by wind-pollinated plants, like grasses, releasing clouds of pollen.

items.prompt: Sycamore seeds have “wings” that spin. How are they dispersed?
items.explain: Spinning slows their fall, so the wind carries them further from the parent tree.
items.hook: Sycamore seeds are **helicopters**: their spinning wings ride the wind.
items.example: Drop a sycamore seed from a step in autumn and watch it twirl away.

items.prompt: Burdock seeds have tiny hooks. How are they dispersed?
items.explain: Velcro was invented after an engineer studied burdock burrs!
items.hook: Hooked seeds are **hitchhikers**, catching a lift on animal fur.
items.example: Burrs stuck in a dog’s fur or on your socks after a country walk are hitchhiking seeds.

items.prompt: In humans, what are the male and female sex cells (gametes) called?
items.explain: Fertilisation happens when a sperm cell joins with an egg cell.
items.hook: Plants: pollen meets ovule. Humans: sperm meets egg. Same idea, different names.

items.prompt: About how long does a human baby develop in the uterus before birth?
items.explain: This time is called gestation.
items.example: Different animals take different times: an elephant carries its baby for nearly two years.

items.prompt: Which organ passes oxygen and nutrients from the mother to the developing baby?
items.explain: The placenta is joined to the baby by the umbilical cord.
items.hook: The placenta is the baby’s **lifeline**: food and oxygen in, waste out, through the umbilical cord.
items.example: Your belly button is where your umbilical cord was once attached.

items.hook: **Cows Moo Softly**: **C**hange one thing, **M**easure one thing, keep everything else the **S**ame.
Mean: **add them all up, then divide by how many** there are.
items.example: Your average score across five spelling tests is a mean.

items.prompt: A measurement that is very close to the true value is…
items.explain: Accurate = close to the true value. Precise = repeat readings are close to each other.
items.hook: **A**ccurate = **A**t the target (the true value).
items.example: Darts all in the bullseye are accurate; darts all clumped together somewhere else are precise but not accurate.

items.prompt: Repeat readings that are all very close to each other are…
items.explain: Readings can be precise but not accurate, for example if a scale always reads 2 g too high.
items.hook: **P**recise = readings **P**acked closely together.
items.example: Kitchen scales that always read 2 g too high give precise but inaccurate results.

items.prompt: A result that doesn’t fit the pattern of the others is called…
items.explain: Check for mistakes, repeat it, and leave it out of the mean if there is a good reason.
items.hook: An anomaly is the **odd one out** that doesn’t fit the pattern.
items.example: In a set of sprint times, one much slower time might be the race when the runner tripped.

items.prompt: If both variables are numbers that can take any value (like temperature and time), which graph should you draw?
items.explain: Use a bar chart when the independent variable is in categories, such as types of material.
items.hook: Numbers on both axes? **Line graph**. Categories (names)? **Bar chart**.
items.example: Weather apps show the temperature through the day as a line graph.

items.prompt: Why do scientists repeat measurements?
items.answer: to make the results more reliable
distractors: to make the experiment fairer to all
because the first one is always wrong
items.explain: Repeats show whether results are consistent.
items.hook: Once could be luck; repeats show whether there is a real pattern.

items.prompt: An idea that can be tested by an experiment is called a…
items.explain: For example: “Sugar dissolves faster in warmer water because the particles move faster.”
items.hook: A hypothesis is a **testable** idea with a reason: “I think… because…”
